title: A spoonful of “original”
opening: I translated a word at breakfast. My neighbour took the wrong pot off the stove. I'd like to try both words on somebody who cooks.
packs: Pack the recipe with the word on the handle
Send the serving spoon with its worn notch
meeting: I put a word under this listening shell. It sounds very grand until there's somebody hungry waiting for it.
traces: The family recipe uses “first” for the pot that boils before the stew. The listener gets the wrong answer if they are looking for the oldest pot.
My neighbour knows the serving spoon by the notch where the handle burned. The mark survives every change of kitchen name.
answers: Record both ways of asking for the pot
Invite the cook to give the instruction at supper
results: The listening shelf now gives both requests. A late visitor tries them out and brings back two different pots.
The cook takes the spoon home and speaks the recipe over a real stove. Her listener signs for the return trip.
returns: I tried the two recorded requests at breakfast. One of them gets you boiled turnips beautifully. The other gets you an empty pot.
A woman who never visits the archive brought us lunch. I wrote her exact instruction inside the old recipe cover.
departure: I'll save you an ear at the Archive of Voices. Listen for the sound of a ladle against a pot.

title: The envelope that came by freight
opening: My sister sent a letter down the freight rail. It arrived faster than the fastest letter train. Keep that to yourself until we've tried it with a full load.
packs: Fasten a paper envelope to the sack
Take the empty travel sack folded flat
meeting: The dispatch clerk gave me a gold sticker for beating the clock. I didn't walk this route to collect stickers.
traces: The envelope went through the narrow letter slot. A full sack would have been taken round the back.
The folded sack fits the short turn. Fill it with dispatch cards and the handle fouls the rail.
answers: Time the porter on the loaded turn
Leave the freight and letter times on separate hooks
results: The porter arrives late with an intact load. Orla pins the corner they had to turn beside the number on the clock.
Two hooks show arrivals by different routes. The clerk can no longer declare a winner without picking a load.
returns: My sister wrote “Try biscuits next time.” There's finally a space on the return slip for what went inside.
I kept the gold sticker. It's holding up the card for the slower route where everyone can read it.
departure: I'll take it to the Civic Machine. If we arrive early, I'm weighing the load before I look at the clock.

title: The view under the trolley
opening: Somebody posted an elegant short route for my cart. If I carry the cart in my arms, I agree it's very short.
packs: Take the crease from a bent route slip
meeting: From the dispatcher’s desk our cart goes clean through that gate. Come down here. It has shoulders.
traces: The chalk ring touches both sides of the turning. The ruling on the map counted the tyres alone.
The slip was bent against a lock while the carrier tried to reach the counter from below.
answers: Lend the rule board to the returning carrier
Draw the working turn on the street map
results: For one shift the carrier moves the board as the cart clears. The waiting line bends differently after supper.
The new turn takes up space on a polished map. A clerk gets to her mother's door with both wheels under her.
returns: The first person to borrow my rule board used it to prop the gate. That worked as well as anything I wrote.
I ran the new turn with the heavy cart. Half an hour later I ate my lunch hot. I kept the wrapper for the surveyor.
departure: I'll walk it to Civic Machine at cart speed. You can catch up with me at dispatch.

title: A corner a small hand can lift
opening: Will you hold this at your knee? My best hanging is perfect for a giant. We've rather run out of giants in the reading room.
packs: Trace the dotted corner onto a little card
meeting: Imani asked me to hang a cover over two words. I'm still waiting to hear which reader she wants to reach them.
traces: The trial hem covers the last word for a seated reader. A taller visitor can lift it and see the whole line.
The card gives a low reader enough purchase, and leaves the oldest knot visible on the other side.
answers: Give the low reader the lift cord
Fit a second, separately fixed corner
results: A reader lifts the full cloth and shows her neighbour what she found. At busy times somebody has to hold the cord.
A new tab fits without undoing the old hem. The slim card takes twice as long to cut as the original hinge.
returns: A girl who came to pull the cord asked for a stool for her granddad. I thought I was making something for her alone.
I took the second corner back to my frame. There's room for my hand there when I sit down at the end of a shift.
departure: I'll carry this to the Nile Archive. Look for the cloth hanging much too high.

title: A substitute’s first bell
opening: I wrote the morning crew into my book last night. This morning half of them have gone to a wedding. The book has better attendance than the workshop.
meeting: The smith knows who should have been here. A duty book with a loose leaf could tell us who was.
traces: The signed rota ends the night before the bell. All the names below it were copied in the same thick ink.
The smooth handle came from the substituted worker's station. Two people remember passing it across the bench.
answers: Give the substitute the first line
Pin the intended crew beside the actual crew
results: The substitute writes a time beside her name. A clerk comes round to ask who covered the last hour.
The double list shows the wedding guests and the workers who held the shop. One name legitimately belongs on both sides.
returns: The substitute’s niece found her in the book. The niece is very proud of the punctuation.
One keeper worked half a shift at the wedding. We kept both entries and sent her a slice of cake.
departure: Meet me at Metalworks when you can. I'll be the one carrying an entire shift under my arm.

title: The weight of a one-word warning
opening: “Clear”, said the visitor. Clear for a person, yes. Bring a parcel in both arms and there's a different afternoon in that word.
packs: Lend Tarin a loaded shoulder strap
meeting: They want the word in the sound archive. They let me choose where to stand when I say it.
traces: The recorded word ends before the cart reaches the passage. The witness can name only the empty walk.
With the load against a shoulder the returning step takes an extra beat. The arch records the catch of breath.
answers: Give the listener the original and a return appointment
Record the two walks from the same mark
results: A visitor can make a second appointment to walk the route with the porter. One word stays open-ended till then.
The archive keeps the empty and loaded steps. A quiet breath between them catches a new listener's ear.
returns: The first listener came back for the walk. She brought her shopping and insisted on carrying it herself.
I never thought I'd recognise my own breath on a shelf. The listener knew which trip was mine.
departure: Come to the Archive of Voices. I'll take the long walk once with my hands free.

title: The seam at the end of a whisper
opening: Someone has sewn a very loud rustle into our recording curtain. The seam is lovely. I am terribly afraid I taught it to the maker.
packs: Make a rubbing of the two old needle holes
meeting: Put that beside a river leaf and listen. Even when the speaker gives permission, an old repair can swallow the next word.
traces: The loose stitch allows the cloth to move without dragging paper across the listening cup.
The rubbed holes mark the fold of the former hinge. It explains the noise in the old recording without touching the original.
answers: Sew a working hinge on a spare screen
Pin the rubbing beside the listening copy
results: The family can record again behind a quieter screen. They reserve the right to leave the original pause alone.
The listener can recognise the cloth sound on the first recording. There is still no guess at what a quiet speaker meant.
returns: The old screen still rustles. The new one doesn't. Every family that comes in gets to choose which to sit behind.
A reader found my little pair of holes and did the listening for herself. I could take a whole evening off.
departure: Meet me in the Nile Archive. Their paper keeps sounds my cloth can hardly hear.

title: Two turns with one quiet hour
opening: I promised that my neighbour could go home early if she took my second bell. I discovered she'd promised somebody else the same hour.
packs: Pack the two shift tags separately
Tie both tags round the idle fitting
meeting: The foreperson put out one stool for two workers. Do we show him the list or wait for the real change of watch?
traces: Both tags show a free hour. The two available hours happen on opposite sides of the same bell.
The fitting stayed on its bench through both shifts. A free person at the wrong end could not take it home.
answers: Let the late worker ring the next bell
Leave the fitting on a rolling stool between shifts
results: The late worker gets a say about the time of the turn. A prompt return now depends on both workers being there.
The work can travel between shifts. Someone has to give up a stool for the working day.
returns: I heard the bell while I was eating and didn't have to run. That is quite a complicated sort of silence.
Our stool travels more than the apprentice. Today the apprentice was home in time to put the bread in.
departure: Find me at Metalworks. If you hear two bells, I'll be standing somewhere in between.
